extracted.intended_audience: manufacturing business owners, plant managers, and industrial executives
extracted.subtask_description: Principles and operational standards for running large-scale manufacturing and finance in industry — covering production planning, vertical integration, pricing, workforce policy, cash management, and contingency response. Geared toward executives designing factory organization and company financial policy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Decentralize final assembly and localize part production
rubrics_metrics.description: Ship parts to assembling stations everywhere and assemble machines locally; wherever a branch can make a part more cheaply than central plant and ship it to them, the branch makes the part.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Original practice: reduced need to crate complete machines for long transport, cut transportation costs, and allowed branches (e.g., Manchester, Cork) to make almost whole products. Anti-pattern: centralizing everything despite higher transport/packing costs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Make each part where it can be produced most economically
rubrics_metrics.description: Each part of a composite article should be made at the exact point where it may be made most economically.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Guides decisions about outsourcing vs in-house—and location of production. Example: branches producing nearly whole cars/tractors when cheaper locally. Emphasizes penny savings accumulating to large annual savings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pursue vertical integration and utilization of by-products
rubrics_metrics.description: Integrate supply and production (mines, coke ovens, blast furnaces, power plant) so waste/by-products (gases, sawdust, coke breeze) are used to fuel operations and generate revenue (fertilizer, benzol).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: River Rouge example: piping gases to boilers, using ammonium sulphate for fertilizer, benzol as motor fuel; reduces fuel purchases and cuts processes out of manufacturing for cost and quality control. Encourages eliminating manual handling and unnecessary intermediate steps.

rubrics_metrics.name: Invest in large-scale, well-located plants for broad economies
rubrics_metrics.description: Develop extensive facilities (e.g., plants with shipping slips, canal/lake access, and space for future development) to cut deeply into costs and achieve large-scale savings across transportation, power generation, casting, and by-product revenues.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: River Rouge planned to accommodate lake steamships and internal logistics to achieve multiple cost savings. Investment can be large (cited $40 million to date) and pay off over time.

rubrics_metrics.name: Continuously experiment with materials to reduce unit costs
rubrics_metrics.description: Constantly experiment with every material that enters into the product (e.g., artificial leather) because small per-unit savings ('a penny here and a penny there') accumulate to large annual savings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Operationalizes continuous improvement and materials R&D at production scale. Encourages in-house trials and substitution to cut costs without harming quality.

rubrics_metrics.name: View machinery and methods as means to increase wealth and create new jobs
rubrics_metrics.description: Improvements that enable one man to do the work of two add to national wealth and typically create new jobs elsewhere; fear of mechanization leading to long-term unemployment is misplaced.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Uses historical analogies (stage-coaches, horse-cabs, shoe machinery) to argue that displaced workers find new employment as industries evolve. Anti-pattern: resisting progress to preserve outdated jobs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not fear saturation; focus on making goods affordable
rubrics_metrics.description: Even if mass production could eventually lead to overproduction, the objective should be to reduce prices and broaden consumption; don't fear a world where everyone has what they want.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Strategy: cut prices as production efficiencies allow, broaden market (e.g., farmers buying more than one car), and rely on public to find new consumptive needs. Practical implication: manage pricing to stimulate demand rather than restrict output.

rubrics_metrics.name: Produce profits by improving methods, not by cutting wages or overcharging
rubrics_metrics.description: Management should produce profits through better methods (brains, improved processes) instead of reducing wages or charging consumers more.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anti-patterns: taking profits out of workers or buyers, cheapening the product, or increasing consumer prices. Emphasizes investment in managerial innovation to capture profit ethically and sustainably.

rubrics_metrics.name: Finance should be subordinate to production — 'finance in the shop, not the bank'
rubrics_metrics.description: The primary focus is production; finance is largely bookkeeping and should be driven by shop performance rather than financial engineering or borrowing to cover operational flaws.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid becoming over-specialized in finance at the expense of production. Example: shop raised funds internally when believed hard up. Warning: mixing banking mentality with business management leads to distortion of purposes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid borrowing to cover mismanagement or waste
rubrics_metrics.description: Borrowing to mask mismanagement or to make up for waste is unsafe; money cannot correct internal operational ailments—economy and brains do.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Borrow for expansion (when business in excellent condition) but not as a poultice for poor operations. Borrowing can be an excuse for laziness and pride; tighten loose places instead of taking loans.

rubrics_metrics.name: The best time to borrow is when you don't need to
rubrics_metrics.description: If borrowing is necessary for expansion, do it when the business is healthy; borrowing when the market perceives you as needing money is the worst time.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: public rumours that money was needed made borrowing harder and dangerous. Maintain lines of credit but keep cash reserves to avoid appearing desperate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Keep substantial cash reserves and lines of credit for emergencies
rubrics_metrics.description: Maintain a large cash balance deposited in various banks and establish lines of credit so borrowing is unnecessary; cash reserves prepare the company to meet contingencies without giving up control.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ford cites cash balances usually in excess of fifty million dollars. Purpose: be ready for emergencies and avoid ceding control of the business through loans.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sell large volume at a small margin rather than few items at a large margin
rubrics_metrics.description: Prefer selling many articles at a small profit to selling few at a large profit; this increases access, employment, production planning, and reduces seasonality and finance needs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Strategy: reduce price to increase market size (example: estimating increase from 500,000 to 800,000 buyers when price reduced), accept temporarily lower profits until economies of scale kick in. Anti-pattern: protecting high prices to the detriment of volume and stability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reinvest profits into the business and limit dividends
rubrics_metrics.description: Treat profits as belonging to the business (to keep it progressive and sound), to employees (who helped produce them), and in part to the public; pay small dividends and reinvest the rest.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Policy: large aggregate profits should be used to improve the business and lower prices rather than distributed to passive stockholders. Example: voluntarily returning money to purchasers when profits unexpectedly high.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer active/working stockholders over passive investors
rubrics_metrics.description: Stockholders should be active in the business and view the company as an instrument of service rather than solely as a cash machine; non-working stockholders are not desirable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rationale: working stockholders will reinvest for service and growth rather than demand maximal dividends. Anti-pattern: having many non-working stockholders pressuring for dividend extraction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treat wages as sacred and avoid reducing them
rubrics_metrics.description: Wages represent family livelihood and social stability; reducing wages is bad financial policy because it reduces buying power and undermines demand.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Balance responsibility between preserving capital for productive enterprise and securing adequate wages for employees. If forced to choose between lowering wages or abolishing dividends, abolish dividends first.

rubrics_metrics.name: Plan production to smooth seasonality and aim for continuous operation
rubrics_metrics.description: Plan production monthly and yearly between sales and production to produce enough so in-transit stock covers orders; educate dealers and consumers to support year-round buying so plants can run continuously.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Continuous production secures skilled mechanics, reduces waste from shutdowns, and improves product through uninterrupted service. Example: campaign to persuade dealers to stock in winter for summer demand.

rubrics_metrics.name: Synchronize production and order streams; avoid large inventories
rubrics_metrics.description: Balance production and orders so that output in transit matches demand; avoid building up finished inventory or excess raw material stocks which tie up capital and incur interest costs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rapid turnover is essential to earn profit on a narrow margin. Overestimating orders when producing at very high daily rates can quickly create millions in unsold inventory — making balancing operations a delicate matter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Maintain contingency capability and short-term stock to survive supplier disruption
rubrics_metrics.description: Have enough internal stock and cross-department coordination to withstand supplier calamities (e.g., supplier plant fire) so production interruptions are minimized.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: after a supplier's plant burned, heads of departments worked extended shifts, made new patterns, leased plants, and furnished equipment; internal stock carried operations over. Encourages preparedness and rapid mobilization.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use price cuts to hasten market adjustment in downturns rather than delay losses
rubrics_metrics.description: In a depressed market, taking immediate price reductions and house-cleaning reduces the duration and depth of the depression; hanging on hopes of higher prices merely increases losses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: 1920 price cuts to bring product within purchasing power; cutting price below cost temporarily to stimulate demand and adjust inventories bought at boom prices. Encourages decisive action to restore harmony between production and buying power.
